issues.detail: Covers mostly the happy path and does not address error scenarios or edge cases such as unparseable files, unsupported languages, tool installation failures, or very large repositories, and the Example 2 output mentions nesting depth and git-history ranking that the instructions never explain how to produce.

scenarios.name: python-hotspots-with-analyzer
scenarios.rationale: Both use lizard with -C 15 -L 100 -w and radon cc -s -n C and exclude migrations and tests, though neither excludes node_modules, vendor, dist, build, __pycache__ or .git. B adds the Critical/Warning/OK tier table and a refactoring order, while A offers only a custom severity script with no tiers, so B covers more of the rubric.

scenarios.name: eslint-cognitive-complexity-setup
scenarios.rationale: B matches the rubric closely: flat config scoped to src/**/*.{js,ts}, both rules at threshold 15, and `npx eslint src/`. It uses 'error' rather than 'warn' but explains the choice. A is more elaborate and has CI extras, but it uses 'error', scopes to .ts/.tsx, runs `npm run lint` instead of `npx eslint src/`, and includes an odd override command. Neither says cognitive complexity is a better readability measure; A only notes that the two metrics count differently.

scenarios.name: manual-cognitive-complexity-count
scenarios.rationale: Both responses compute cyclomatic 6 and cognitive 9 with correct per-construct breakdowns, but neither mentions the else in the cyclomatic list differently; A omits the explicit OK (<15) classification that B includes, while B's ordering is slightly less clean, so B edges out on rubric coverage.
